focus: Paired Fagales lesson: Juglandaceae/Juglans versus Fagaceae/Quercus

Juglandaceae.where_to_look_first: Start with the leaves: local walnuts have alternate pinnately compound aromatic leaves. Then confirm male catkins and a one-seeded nut enclosed by a husk.
core_characters: Trees with pinnately compound leaves; stipules absent.
Leaves often aromatic/resinous when crushed and may bear glandular scales/hairs.
Flowers unisexual; male flowers commonly in catkins.
Juglans female flowers occur in short terminal clusters/spikes on current growth.
Fruit contains one seed/nut, surrounded by a fleshy or fibrous husk/perianth-derived outer layer.
Juglans twigs may show chambered pith.

Fagaceae.where_to_look_first: Start with the fruit: a nut/acorn subtended or partly enclosed by a scaly cupule. Leaves are simple, not pinnately compound.
core_characters: Trees/shrubs with alternate simple leaves and stipules.
Flowers unisexual; male flowers commonly borne in catkins.
Fruit is a nut associated with a cupule.
Quercus is especially recognizable by an acorn with a scaly cup.
Leaf undersides commonly have stellate hairs in many species.

fast_key: Pinnately compound leaf + aromatic walnut foliage + husked nut → Juglandaceae.
Simple leaf + acorn/nut sitting in a cupule → Fagaceae.
Both can have male catkins, so catkins alone do not separate them.

cards.look_here_first: Start with the long odd-pinnately compound leaf with many narrow leaflets; then look for the marble-sized husked walnut.
confirm: Alternate odd-pinnately compound leaves with many narrow lanceolate leaflets.
Leaves aromatic when crushed in Forest Service descriptions.
Monoecious: slender male catkins arise on previous-year wood.
Female flowers occur singly or in short terminal clusters on current year's growth.
Fruit is small and globose with a fibrous outer husk and a hard deeply grooved nut.
Twigs and buds are useful secondary characters.
cards.tie_breaker: Against oaks: compound leaf and husked walnut. Against J. major: use leaflet count/width, fruit size and overlap-zone caution.

cards.look_here_first: If fruit is present, find the scaly cupule beneath the nut/acorn. Then use leaf, bud, bark and cupule details for species-level ID.
cards.note: Fagaceae already passed the Joey audit as sufficient; this paired module exists mainly so Juglandaceae is taught against a strong familiar oak reference.

common_mistakes: Calling any tree with catkins an oak or walnut—both families can have catkins.
Using nut shape alone without checking whether there is a cupule versus a husk.
Forgetting that Juglandaceae leaves are compound while local Quercus leaves are simple.
